name: Collagen induction therapy

card.summary: Microneedling: controlled skin punctures meant to trigger collagen repair; the best-studied use is scars, with more modest evidence for wrinkles and texture.
card.aka: Microneedling, dermarolling, skin needling, percutaneous collagen induction (PCI)
card.note: Non-clinical settings with poor infection control have been linked to blood-borne infection outbreaks when combined with blood-derived products.

quick.overview:
Collagen induction therapy, usually called microneedling, uses a roller, stamp or motorised pen studded with fine needles to puncture the skin many times. The aim is to provoke a wound-healing response that produces new collagen and elastin without removing the epidermis.

It is used for acne and other scars, stretch marks, fine lines, skin laxity and general skin texture. Published studies, mostly small or retrospective, report improvement in scars and some photoaging, while larger controlled evidence is more limited.
quick.mechanism: Needle punctures create micro-channels and tiny injuries in the dermis. Proponents and authors of the early clinical papers describe a healing cascade of inflammation, fibroblast activity and new collagen deposition over weeks to months, with the epidermis left largely intact.
quick.risks: Reported effects include redness, swelling, pinpoint bleeding and temporary irritation. Infections, pigment changes and scarring have been described in complication reviews, and public-health authorities have warned about blood-borne infection when needling is paired with blood-derived products in unregulated settings. Professional microneedling devices are regulated as medical devices in the US; home devices vary widely.

lead: Collagen induction therapy (CIT), widely known as microneedling, dermarolling or skin needling, is a cosmetic procedure in which a device bearing fine needles repeatedly punctures the skin to create controlled micro-injuries [1][11]. The intended result is stimulation of the skin's repair processes and new collagen and elastin formation, as an alternative to ablative treatments that remove the epidermis [2][3].

It is used for acne and other scars, stretch marks, wrinkles, photoaging and skin laxity, and is discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a skin-quality and scar treatment. Published clinical work includes retrospective series, small trials and case reports describing improvement in scars, burn scars, striae and upper-lip wrinkles [2][5][7][9][10].

Reviews of procedural complications and later literature note that evidence quality varies, that device and protocol standardisation is lacking, and that infection-control failures in non-clinical settings have caused harm [8][11].

paras: Devices include hand-held rollers, stamps and electric pens with needle lengths commonly described as between about 0.5 and 2.5 mm, with depth chosen by treatment area and goal [1]. Sessions are generally described as being repeated several weeks apart, with visible changes reported to develop over months [1].
A related practice combines needling with topical products or with platelet-rich plasma (PRP), sometimes marketed as a vampire facial [11].

Proponents describe a controlled wound-healing response: platelet activation and cytokine release, followed by fibroblast proliferation and collagen and elastin synthesis, with remodelling over months [1][2]. The authors of the early percutaneous collagen induction papers stressed that the epidermis is preserved, in contrast to ablative laser or peel methods that can cause pigment changes [2][4]. The clinical papers cited here report outcomes and some histology rather than settling the mechanism in detail.

According to Grokipedia, the technique originated in the 1990s with South African plastic surgeon Desmond Fernandes, followed by a roller device from German inventor Horst Liebl around 2000 and automated pens from 2010 [1]; these details come from a single AI-generated source. A 2008 retrospective analysis of 480 patients treated with percutaneous collagen induction was a widely cited milestone [2]. Grokipedia also says the US FDA classified aesthetic microneedling devices as Class II in 2018 [1].

Expected short-term effects include erythema, swelling and transient discomfort [1]. A review of complications from cutaneous aesthetic procedures lists infection, pigmentation changes and other adverse events across devices and techniques [8].

Wikipedia reports that health authorities have raised concern about needling combined with PRP in non-medical settings; in 2018 the New Mexico Department of Health warned of possible blood-borne infection spread, and in April 2024 the CDC reported three women diagnosed with HIV after vampire facials at an Albuquerque spa [11].

A retrospective analysis of 480 patients treated between 1997 and 2006 reported improvement of scars, wrinkles and skin laxity with percutaneous collagen induction [2]. Related papers by the same group discussed photoaging and a study aimed at whether the technique avoids dyspigmentation [3][4]. A study in burn scars [5] and a report on striae distensae [7] also described improvement, and a case report described treatment of burn-scar contracture [6]. A study of upper-lip wrinkles [9] and a 2020 evaluation in facial scars [10] reported benefits. A 2022 review covers microneedling-associated procedures for facial rejuvenation [12].

Registered trials include comparisons against silicone sheeting for hypertrophic scars [13] and against fractional non-ablative laser for stretch marks [14], and a pilot of microneedling combined with a filler for acne scars [15]. Many published studies are small, uncontrolled or retrospective.

timeline.event: Grokipedia attributes invention to Desmond Fernandes, who used a tattoo-gun-like device for scars [1].
Dermaroller introduced in Europe, per Grokipedia [1].
Retrospective series of 480 patients on percutaneous collagen induction published [2].
Automated pen devices introduced, per Grokipedia [1].
Microneedling devices classified as Class II medical devices in the US, per Grokipedia [1].
CDC reports HIV cases linked to a New Mexico spa offering vampire facials [11].

lore.intro: Microneedling is discussed in skin and beauty communities as a scar and texture treatment, often via at-home rollers and pens; no forum threads are cited here.

claims.claim: Microneedling boosts collagen and improves scars.
claims.believers: Proponents say repeated needling triggers new collagen and fades acne scars and stretch marks over several sessions.
claims.experts: Published retrospective series and small trials report scar and striae improvement [2][5][7], with limitations in design and size.

claims.claim: Microneedling avoids the pigmentation risk of lasers and peels.
claims.believers: Proponents say the epidermis stays largely intact, so darker skin tones can be treated.
claims.experts: An early study set out to test this claim [4], while a complication review lists pigment change among reported events [8].

claims.claim: Microneedling with PRP or topicals gives better results.
claims.believers: Users and clinics promote add-ons such as PRP.
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that whether PRP adds benefit remains uncertain, and that unregulated vampire facials have been linked to HIV infections [11].
